text: Ask Claude for a deck, and you get a deck.
Felix Riesberg, an engineering manager at Anthropik, would send a short seller after
it.
On his blog he calls this range drawing on several fields, not just the one the task
seems to need.
Now that multi-agent setups are easier to run, he's seen really interesting results
asking Claude to bring in extra fields.
This first trick is an old one from The Art of Innovation by Tom Kelly and Jonathan Littman.
Replace the noun with verbs.
A quarterly review isn't a deck.
It's getting busy people to believe a story about cause and effect, and to decide under
uncertainty in 30 minutes.
The verbs make it easier for you and Claude to see which fields could add a useful angle.
His second trick is what every heist movie spends its first half hour on.
Assemble the crew.
Felix pretends the deck has to be amazing, or aliens blow up Earth.
For production quality he'd bring in an analyst, a journalist, and an editor.
If it gets presented, a motion and audio designer too.
Then a red team to attack it.
A short seller and a forensic accountant.
He admits this takes creativity.
Until his colleague Alex Albert used Blender to render interior designs, he'd never thought
of using Claude for 3D environments on his homepage.
And he's made video games before.
His homepage is a 3D room now.
He says this is where he sees the most magic.
Before your next big ask, write the verbs, then name the crew.
And have Claude do what a short seller does to research a position, not write like one.
Roleplay makes the transcript weirder, not the result better.
Who joins your crew first?
The short seller or the forensic accountant?
